sources.entry: Optimizing subroutines in assembly language - Shows which chains renaming cannot break, from partial registers to flags, and the zero-cost idioms that do.

summary.title: Optimizing subroutines in assembly language
summary.one_liner: Learn how to combine x86/x86-64 assembly with high-level code and optimize CPU-intensive subroutines, including out-of-order execution, dependency-chain breaking, loops, and vector code.
keywords: when to write assembly instead of compiler
takeaways: Assembly is still useful for checking compiler output, but modern compilers often beat hand-written assembly for speed.
Covers ABI register usage, calling conventions, and how to link assembly with C++ via inline assembly and intrinsics.
Explains out-of-order execution, instruction latency and throughput, and how to break dependency chains.
Includes sections on loops (overhead, bottleneck analysis, unrolling, AVX512 mask registers) and vector programming.
summary.summary: This is the second of five manuals by Agner Fog, aimed at advanced assembly programmers and compiler makers. The table of contents covers ABI and calling conventions, inline assembly and intrinsics, linking libraries, and optimizing for speed and size. Speed topics include out-of-order execution, dependency chains, jumps and calls, loop bottleneck analysis, and vector code with AVX and AVX512. The manual refers readers to companion manuals for C++ optimization, microarchitecture, instruction tables, and calling conventions.
